pending_items.title: Meet the Pacific Islanders standing for Palestine against Christian Zionism
pending_items.content:
Michel Mulipola is a comic book artist and former professional wrestler. He’s also an activist for indigenous self-determination in Palestine and across the Pacific Islands, as well as a former Green Party candidate in New Zealand.

It’s in keeping with his family history. Mulipola’s great-grandfather, Mataʻutia Karauna Solomona, was a Samoan resistance leader and secretary of the Mau movement, which sought to free Western Samoa of colonial rule in the 1920s and 1930s.

Solomona’s arrest resulted in a massacre of unarmed protesters by the New Zealand military and police.

“So, I guess activism or even just fighting for freedom, for sovereignty, is in my blood,” says Mulipola, who has received media attention for his customised image of the Palestinian flag using traditional Samoan petroglyphs.

The artwork, which incorporates symbols drawn from Samoan cultural traditions, became a way for Mulipola to explain why he believed his people should stand with Palestinians.

Samoans around the world grew more curious, and have carried the flag at Palestine demonstrations. But the response was not all positive.

“Christian Zionism has got quite a strong stranglehold on Samoans and other people of the Pacific,” Mulipola tells Middle East Eye in a video call interview.

A self-described atheist, Mulipola was accused of not being truly Samoan, just because he did not support Israel.

'Christian Zionism has got quite a strong stranglehold on Samoans and other people of the Pacific'

- Michel Mulipola, comic book artist and activist

These reactions exposed a deeper tension present in the Pacific islands since even before the start of Israel’s genocide in Gaza .

A small but growing number of mainly young Pasifika intellectuals, theologians, and activists are pushing back against decades of deep missionary and elder evangelical conditioning.

This conditioning, heavily influenced by Christian Zionists from the United States , saw support for Israel become intertwined with local cultural identity, so that questioning someone’s political beliefs came to feel like questioning one’s own people.

Across the Pacific, a region with diverse Indigenous cultures, histories and Christian traditions, activists and church leaders' arguments are not simply about Palestine.

They are also about how communities understand colonialism, Indigenous identity, religious authority and the right of peoples to determine their own futures.

The Pacific's relationship with Christianity is complex. Missionaries arrived in many islands from the late 18th century onwards, and the religion became deeply embedded in the social and cultural life of many communities.

But the growth of Christian Zionism in the region is something different.

According to Reverend James Bhagwan, general secretary of the Pacific Conference of Churches (PCC), which represents churches of mixed Indo-Fijian and other heritages, the more recent growth of Christian Zionism has taken place alongside the expansion of newer evangelical and Pentecostal movements.

“Christian Zionism is not a new thing. It has been slowly creeping into different spaces over the last 40 years,” he says.

Bhagwan’s ecumenical organisation brings together 35 national denominations and 11 national councils of churches across 20 Pacific Island states and territories.

Its work includes advocating for Indigenous self-determination in places such as West Papua, New Caledonia (Kanaky) and French Polynesia.

For Bhagwan, that work creates a moral obligation to engage with Palestine, too.

“We cannot pick and choose what self-determination we support,” he said. The Methodist minister believes that some Pacific Christians have difficulty distinguishing between the Israel described in biblical texts, the modern state of Israel, Judaism and Zionism.

In his view, this can lead to political positions being formed through religious identification rather than a fuller understanding of the realities facing Palestinians.

Along with Bhagwan, Mulipola points to a lack of awareness about Palestinian Christians.

He told a story about Brian Tamaki, the leader of Destiny Church, a conservative Pentecostal movement founded in New Zealand. Tamaki has led pro-Israel rallies in New Zealand.

“I remember they were counter-protesting a Palestine action, and he was spouting off his hateful Christian rhetoric,” Mulipola recalls. “My good friend Rand Hazel jumped on the megaphone and said: ‘I’m a Palestinian Christian, born in Jerusalem, my people spoke Aramaic, the language of Jesus…’ and Tamaki was gobsmacked.”

Some communities, he says, have been taken in by Eurocentric propaganda portraying all Palestinians as Muslims and demanding unconditional support for the gathering of all Jews in the holy land.

In Fiji, journalist and activist Mara Mahoney says the connection between religious belief and national identity can be particularly difficult to challenge.

Mahoney grew up in the village of Savusavu on evangelical Christian Bible study, church attendance and Christian schooling, which shaped her understanding of the world from an early age.

'When you're trying to speak facts with people… you're trying to talk about the Nakba… people will just be like, well, who are we to question God?'

She recalls being taught that Israel was home to God's chosen people, and that some Fijians descended from the lost tribes of Israel, a belief that could make questioning support for the modern Israeli state feel like questioning one’s own faith.

Mahoney’s own political awakening came when she left her hometown to study at the University of Hawaii at Manoa. It was there that she learned about colonialism and Indigenous struggles in the Pacific, including those in Hawaii, West Papua and New Caledonia (Kanaky).

She says missionaries had used Fijian oral storytelling and pseudo-genealogical traditions to construct narratives connecting Fijian origins to Israel. These stories, Mahoney argues, were subsequently presented to communities as accounts of their own ancestry.

The historical question is significant, but it requires careful treatment. Research by anthropologist Lynda Newland documents how missionary ideas about Fijian origins and the lost tribes of Israel developed between 1835 and Fiji's cession to Britain in 1874.

Newland's research establishes that these ideas have a historical basis in missionary discourse and that they became influential among some Indigenous Fijian clans and church groups.

For Mahoney, these narratives help explain why some Fijians find it harder to question political positions associated with that connection.

“When you're trying to speak facts with people… you're trying to talk about the Nakba… people will just be like, well, who are we to question God?” she says.

The issue is not simply that people hold a religious belief, Mahoney argues. It is that questioning the belief can mean confronting an entire system of education, family expectations and identity.

“The Christianity that was kind of brought to our shores was built on fear,” Mulipola says.

“You hear people calling themselves God-fearing people, and I'm like, I've never liked that term because ruling through fear is dangerous.

“It's manipulative. It's not a loving relationship. It's an abusive one. And so many people fear the repercussions of speaking up or speaking against it.”

Mulipola describes the Samoan concept of fa'aaloalo, often associated with respect and deference, as one factor shaping how people respond to authority and adhere to Christian Zionism.

In his interpretation, the expectation to respect elders and authority figures can reinforce a reluctance to question religious leaders or teachings. Mahoney says a similar dynamic exists in Fiji.

Mulipola believes this dynamic has been compounded by forms of Christianity introduced through colonial rule, in which obedience and unquestioning faith can become closely linked.

The connection between the former wrestler's family history and the Palestinian struggle is not merely symbolic. He sees both as struggles over sovereignty, dignity and the right of a people to determine their future.

'You hear people calling themselves God-fearing people, and I'm like, I've never liked that term because ruling through fear is dangerous'

Pacific concerns for family and community, he argues, are not incompatible with supporting Palestinians.

pending_items.title: Israel’s Eisenkot slams ‘Jewish terrorism’ after attacks by settlers in West Bank
pending_items.content:
Israeli ​militant settlers attacked Palestinian villages in the occupied West Bank early on Sunday, starting fires and scrawling racist graffiti, residents said, prompting an accusation of "Jewish terrorism" from the man trying to form an Israeli government.

The attacks, the latest in an escalation that began after Hamas launched attacks ​on Israel from ‌the Gaza Strip in 2023, come nearly a month after an inconclusive election stripped incumbent Prime Minister ⁠Benjamin Netanyahu of his majority.

Opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has been asked to form a government, though his prospects seem little better.

Reuters saw burned-out Palestinian vehicles and walls spray-painted with slogans ‌such as "Revenge" and "Death to Arabs" in villages near Ramallah. No one immediately claimed responsibility and no injuries were ⁠reported.

Eisenkot called the attacks "Jewish terrorism", saying that "extremist groups that set fire to vehicles and homes are undermining regional stability, putting lives at risk and doing grave damage to Israel's national security and foreign relations".

He said the policies of ​Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich , ultra-nationalist ministers in Netanyahu's cabinet, had "brought the area to the brink of anarchy, ‌and the authorities have yet to address the crisis".

To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.

One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.

Netanyahu has not yet commented but Foreign Minister Gideon Saar condemned the attacks by a "handful of extremists" and said they are "against our values and do not represent the law-abiding citizens of Judea and Samaria", the biblical names for the West Bank.

"Israeli ‌authorities are firmly committed to enforcing the law against extremist violence," he told the ELNET Jerusalem Summit.

UN bodies and most countries of the world deny the legality of the ​settlements, which make the prospect of an independent Palestinian state ever more remote, a position Israel disputes.

Read more 'We see our culture being stolen': How Israeli settlers are attacking West Bank olive groves

Israeli police said they opened an investigation into the attacks, while the military condemned the violence, saying soldiers and police had been dispatched to the areas ​of Deir as-Sudan, Deir Abu Masha'al, Kafr Malik and At-Tuwani "following reports and footage showing vehicles being set on fire and graffiti being sprayed ​in the area".

Ben-Gvir replied in an X post that Eisenkot's condemnation amounted to selling out ​to Arab parties, which could become part of a possible new government. Smotrich favours settlement expansion and wants Israel to annex the West Bank.

Yousef Jabareen, head of the Joint List, the ​largest Arab party in Israel's parliament, said the attacks were "the direct result of the deepening occupation and a government policy under which violence against Palestinians has become an everyday occurrence", citing encouragement from Ben-Gvir and Smotrich.

Israel's parliament was sworn in on November 10 without a new government, after the election on October 27 stripped Netanyahu of his majority but left others with no clear path to power.

Read more Eisenkot invites Netanyahu’s party for ‘marathon’ Israeli coalition talks

President Isaac Herzog has ⁠tasked Eisenkot, who heads the centre-right Yashar, with forming a government, while Netanyahu remains caretaker prime minister.

Unless Eisenkot forms a unity government with Netanyahu, he is likely to ⁠need support from Arab ​parties to be able to count on a majority of parliament's 120 seats.

If no one is able to form a government, another election will be held next year.
